documents.unit: Center for Excellence in Teaching and Learning (CETL)
documents.title: AI Guidelines (archived copy)
documents.summary: A teaching-center page that shares Idaho statewide principles for generative AI, advises instructors to decide and explain their own AI rules in the syllabus, lists possible student and instructor uses, and offers three syllabus templates. It takes no institutional stance and is advisory.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule of its own: "Our goal is ... not to advocate for or against your use or your students use of such tools". It tells instructors "Your Decisions" (not use / use) and offers three syllabus examples from "No AI Allowed" to "Unconditional AI Allowed", so the stance is delegates with tiers.

units.why: The center states it will "offer workshops and consultations on AI’s uses and limitations for faculty", which is faculty support for learning about AI, so P63.
units.anchor: offer workshops and consultations on AI’s uses and limitations for faculty

units.why: CETL says it takes part in "SBoE and multi-institutional working groups", an engagement with peers and the state board, so P88 (coalitions) rather than P63.
units.anchor: involved in SBoE and multi-institutional working groups to advance our knowledge

units.why: CETL "sponsor[s] a cross-disciplinary AI faculty group", a faculty community for learning about AI, which is P63.
units.anchor: sponsor a cross-disciplinary AI faculty group, now in its second year

units.why: The page states its purpose and scope ("summarize, share, and invite information and recommendations on ... best practices"), a framing statement, so P56; it is not itself a rule.
units.anchor: summarize, share, and invite information and recommendations on existing and emerging best practices for AI
units.fit_note: Page purpose statement rather than an institution-wide framework with principles.

units.why: It says who made the principles and when ("created by members of the Idaho Statewide AI Alliance in January 2024"), so P84 describes how the guidance was made.
units.anchor: created by members of the Idaho Statewide AI Alliance in January 2024

units.why: The shared principles set an institution-level statement of purpose and values ("human judgment, empathy, and ethical discernment"), which is a framework, P56.
units.anchor: focus on human judgment, empathy, and ethical discernment when harnessing generative AI

units.why: The principles are non-binding ("not hard and fast rules") but users are told it is "a good idea" to keep them in mind, a recommendation attached to the framework, so P56 with should.
units.anchor: not hard and fast rules, it is a good idea to review them
units.fit_note: States that the framework is advisory, not binding.

units.why: The first listed principle ("People come first.") is a statement of values inside the shared framework, so P56.
units.anchor: People come first.

units.why: The principle that "an inquiry mindset will foster a culture of continuous learning about AI" encourages users to keep learning about AI, so P102 rather than P56.
units.anchor: An inquiry mindset will foster a culture of continuous learning about AI.
units.fit_note: Framed as a principle, not a stated duty.

units.why: "Learners need equitable access to generative AI" is an equity and access principle, matching P51.
units.anchor: Learners need equitable access to generative AI.

units.why: This principle ("Responsive, engaged teaching matters more than ever") is a value statement in the framework, so P56.
units.anchor: Responsive, engaged teaching matters more than ever.

units.why: The principle says "expectations around privacy and copyright are evolving rapidly", a point about copyright and privacy, closest to P52.
units.anchor: Expectations around privacy and copyright are evolving rapidly.
units.fit_note: Also covers privacy, which P52 does not.

units.why: The principle "Transparency is essential" in a list about using generative AI points toward disclosing AI use; it is stated as a value, so P24 with informs.
units.anchor: Transparency is essential.
units.fit_note: Stated as a principle; the text does not say what must be disclosed.

units.why: The Alliance calls its statement "a living document that will likely be modified in the future", which is a revisit-regularly policy, P54.
units.anchor: a living document that will likely be modified in the future

units.why: It names the source the Alliance drew on ("used a statement published by the United Nations Internet Governance Forum"), describing how the statement was made, P84.
units.anchor: used a statement published by the United Nations Internet Governance Forum

units.why: The page lists "help generate ideas" among uses of AI, a permitted brainstorming use (P15), stated with "One can use" so modality may.
units.anchor: One can use AI to help generate ideas

units.why: The same sentence lists AI as "a grammar and spelling checker" and a tool "to moderate voice and tone in writing", an editing permission, P91.
units.anchor: as a grammar and spelling checker, as a tool to moderate voice and tone

units.why: AI as a "virtual study-buddy to bounce ideas off of" is a tutor-like use for understanding, closest to P12 (P15 brainstorming is the other candidate; the study-buddy framing decides).
units.anchor: or even as a virtual study-buddy to bounce ideas off of to see what sticks
units.fit_note: Combines study help and idea bouncing.

units.why: The text warns AI can let learners "pass a class without having to do the hard work of learning", the skill-building rationale for limiting AI, P41.
units.anchor: pass a class without having to do the hard work of learning something

units.why: Educators "need to be transparent about our goals" and "the rationale we have for our decisions", i.e. give students reasons behind AI rules, which is P66.
units.anchor: we need to be transparent about our goals for our learners

units.why: The page recommends "a shift towards a 'flipped classroom' model" as a response to AI, a course redesign, P35.
units.anchor: a shift towards a “flipped classroom” model

units.why: Case studies and project-based learning are suggested as venues where AI is absent or used "under your direction", an assignment redesign around AI, P35.
units.anchor: Working on case studies, project based learning, and other high impact practices

units.why: It says AI should move teaching "beyond the compilation of factual knowledge" toward problem solving, a rethinking of what is assessed and taught, P35.
units.anchor: move beyond the compilation of factual knowledge as a marker of an education

units.why: The page leaves it to the instructor to decide whether to ban AI ("you may conclude that you will not allow them to use AI tools"), so P04.
units.anchor: you may conclude that you will not allow them to use AI tools

units.why: The condition for a ban is that AI "will jeopardize their ability" to develop skills, which is the skill-building rationale, P41.
units.anchor: use of AI tools will jeopardize their ability to do so

units.why: Instructors who ban AI are told to "clearly explain your decision ... in your instructions and on your syllabus", an expectation to state the AI rule in syllabus and assignment instructions, P09.
units.anchor: clearly explain your decision and the reasoning for your decision

units.why: Instructors banning AI are advised that "citing the Student Code of Conduct E-1.c would be useful", tying a ban to the misconduct code, P36.
units.anchor: citing the Student Code of Conduct E-1.c would be useful
units.policy: Instructors who ban AI should find it useful to cite Student Code of Conduct E-1.c in the syllabus.
units.fit_note: Advice to cite the code; the text does not itself say AI misuse is misconduct.

units.why: Instructors who allow AI "should communicate your policy in your syllabus, and on the instructions for your assignments", the syllabus-statement expectation, P09.
units.anchor: You should communicate your policy in your syllabus

units.why: Instructors who allow AI should "explain what you will not allow and the reasoning", giving students the reasons behind limits, P66.
units.anchor: Also, explain what you will not allow and the reasoning for your decision.

units.why: Under "Brainstorm topics" the page lists AI for topics, narrowing questions and getting started ideas, a brainstorming use (P15).
units.anchor: query AI text generators to provide potential research topics, narrow the focus of research questions

units.why: "Create an Outline" for "writing or coding" is outlining support, P91 (outlining is named in its definition).
units.anchor: An AI text generator can provide an outline for writing or coding

units.why: "Proofread" and suggesting alternative expressions is proofreading and editing support, P91.
units.anchor: use an AI text generator to proofread writing

units.why: "Collect Sources" with "annotated bibliographies" is a permitted use for finding source material, which no existing type names.
units.anchor: AI text generators can create annotated bibliographies
units.uncovered_note: AI used to find and annotate primary and secondary sources for research.

units.why: A learner drafts with AI and compares it with a rubric to "internalize the evaluation standards", a self-check study use, P14.
units.anchor: create a draft of a writing or coding prompt to compare it
units.fit_note: Self-check against a rubric in a norming session; the draft is AI output used as a comparison object.

units.why: "Practice Analysis": learners compare their own analysis with an AI-generated one, a practice and self-check use, P14.
units.anchor: AI text generators can provide an analysis of themes in a piece of writing

units.why: The page says it is "perfectly acceptable not to use" text generators in teaching, so instructors may decline; this belongs with instructor AI use (P59).
units.anchor: It’s perfectly acceptable not to use them
units.fit_note: Permission to abstain from AI rather than a use.

units.why: Instructors are told text generators give "some options to use in their practice" (outcomes, rubrics, materials, course outlines), an instructor-use permission, P59.
units.anchor: Text generators also give instructors some options to use in their practice.

units.why: Generating learning outcomes is listed as an instructor use of AI, P59.
units.anchor: Generating learning outcomes

units.why: Instructors "need to use your own expertise to review the generated outcomes", verification of AI output, P31.
units.anchor: You will need to use your own expertise to review the generated outcomes
units.fit_note: Applies to instructors reviewing AI-generated outcomes.

units.why: Creating assignment rubrics is listed as an instructor use of AI, P59.
units.anchor: Creating assignment rubrics

units.why: For rubrics, instructors are told to "use your own judgement when creating the finalized version", critical review of AI output, P31.
units.anchor: use your own judgement when creating the finalized version
units.fit_note: Applies to instructors reviewing AI-drafted rubrics.

units.why: Identifying learning materials is listed as an instructor use of AI, P59.
units.anchor: Identifying learning materials

units.why: It warns that text generators have "a deserved reputation for making up source material", so output must be treated critically, P31.
units.anchor: Text generators have a deserved reputation for making up source material
units.fit_note: Warning rather than an explicit duty to verify.

units.why: Outlining a course is listed as an instructor use of AI, P59.
units.anchor: Outlining a Course

units.why: Instructors "still must play an integral role in all of these generative processes" and keep the "final say", human oversight of AI-assisted course work, P59.
units.anchor: Note that you still must play an integral role in all of these generative processes.
units.fit_note: Adds a requirement of instructor oversight which P59 does not name.

units.why: It says "It is important to be transparent when using large language model generative AI applications in your work", a disclosure expectation, P24.
units.anchor: It is important to be transparent when using large language model generative AI applications

units.why: The page notes the difficulty that the chat is "not retrievable by others" when citing, which bears on how AI citations must capture the prompt and output, closest to P25.
units.anchor: the “chat” in applications like ChatGPT are not retrievable by others
units.fit_note: States a citation difficulty; it does not itself require prompt or output details.

units.why: It points to APA, Chicago and MLA recommendations for citing AI, and users "may have to make your own decision", a citation guidance unit, P25.
units.anchor: Style guides such APA, Chicago Manual of Style, and MLA have recommendations
units.fit_note: Defers to external style guides; no specific tool, prompt or date requirement.

units.why: "The key is to be transparent" about referencing AI use, with the form left to the user, a disclosure expectation, P24.
units.anchor: the key is to be transparent

units.why: CETL offers three syllabus templates (no AI, some AI, unconditional AI) by "level of AI utilization", named tiers, P05.
units.anchor: three examples of language you can include in your syllabus

units.why: The unconditional-AI template links to citation practices in Chicago, APA and MLA, so unconditional use still comes with citation guidance, P25.
units.anchor: links to suggested citation practices in the Chicago Manual of Style, APA
units.fit_note: Citation links only, with no required details.

units.why: CETL says it will not "advocate for or against" AI use, leaving the decision to instructors and students, which is P04 rather than P03.
units.anchor: not to advocate for or against your use or your students use of such tools
units.fit_note: Institutional neutrality, not a rule that the instructor decides.

units.why: The center invites feedback ("We welcome your feedback and collaboration"), a feedback channel on the guidance, P54.
units.anchor: We welcome your feedback and collaboration on this issue.

units.why: A recorded workshop titled "Engineering Effective Prompts for AI" is offered as a resource on prompting, P93.
units.anchor: Chat With Me: Engineering Effective Prompts for AI
units.fit_note: A resource listing, not advice text.

units.why: The page lists "Previously Recorded CETL Workshops" on AI for faculty (teaching tools, syllabus, roundtable), faculty support, P63.
units.anchor: Previously Recorded CETL Workshops

units.why: The page names "Zoom AI Companion" under Software Resources, pointing to an institution-provided AI tool, P92.
units.anchor: Zoom AI Companion
units.fit_note: Listed without conditions of use.

units.why: Under Software Resources the page lists "AI detection feature through Turnitin for Canvas Assignments", a detection tool offered, P40.
units.anchor: AI detection feature through Turnitin for Canvas Assignments
units.fit_note: Listed as a resource with no guidance on reliability or evidence.

documents.title: Syllabus Language for AI
documents.summary: A knowledge-base article from the Center for Teaching & Learning with three ready-to-paste syllabus statements: AI prohibited, AI only with prior instructor permission, and AI allowed with citation and a short note. Each ties violations to the Student Code of Conduct.
documents.stance_why: The article offers three options and says "please choose one or specify your own", so the university sets no single stance and hands the choice to instructors; the options ("AI Use Prohibited", "AI with Prior Permission", "AI with Acknowledgement") are tiers.

units.why: The template tells instructors "please choose one or specify your own" of three options, a named set of tiers, so P05.
units.anchor: (please choose one or specify your own)

units.why: The boilerplate says it "is important to clarify how they may or may not be used in this course", the aim of stating an AI rule in the syllabus, P09.
units.anchor: important to clarify how they may or may not be used in this course
units.fit_note: Appears in all three options; coded once.

units.why: The text defines scope by listing "ChatGPT, Copilot, Perplexity, Grammarly, image generators, and automated coding/writing assistants", a definition of AI tools covered, P61.
units.anchor: including but not limited to ChatGPT, Copilot, Perplexity, Grammarly, image generators, and automated coding/writing assistants
units.fit_note: Appears in all three options; coded once. Includes Grammarly and coding assistants.

units.why: Option 1 says AI tools "[are] not permitted in this course", a default ban, P01.
units.anchor: assistants—is not permitted in this course

units.why: Option 1 classes unauthorized AI use as "a form of unauthorized assistance", a misconduct classification, P36.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of AI tools is considered a form of unauthorized assistance

units.why: Option 1 grounds the ban in skill-building: the course "build[s] foundational skills ... that require your direct engagement", so P41.
units.anchor: intentionally designed to build foundational skills

units.why: It says using AI "to generate or revise work may hinder the achievement of these objectives", the practice-shortcut rationale, P41.
units.anchor: Using AI tools to generate or revise work may hinder the achievement of these objectives

units.why: Even under the ban, AI is allowed where "explicitly allowed by the instructor for a specific assignment", so the instructor can allow it per assignment, P04.
units.anchor: unless explicitly allowed by the instructor for a specific assignment

units.why: Option 1 says prohibited AI use "will be treated as a violation of academic integrity" with sanctions under the Code, P36.
units.anchor: will be treated as a violation of academic integrity and may result in sanctions

units.why: Students "are responsible for reviewing and adhering to all university policies regarding academic honesty", binding AI use to existing policy, P77.
units.anchor: responsible for reviewing and adhering to all university policies regarding academic honesty

units.why: Option 2 sets the rule when no permission is given: "all assignments must be completed independently and without assistance from automated tools", a fallback ban, P06.
units.anchor: Unless permission is explicitly granted, all assignments must be completed independently

units.why: Option 2 requires students to "email a description of your AI request to your instructor" before the work, asking first, P10.
units.anchor: Email a description of your AI request to your instructor
units.fit_note: Mandatory pre-approval request, stronger than 'ask when unsure'.

units.why: If permission is given, students "must ... cite any AI-generated material" in a recognized format, a disclosure duty, P24.
units.anchor: cite any AI-generated material using a clear attribution and appropriate citation format

units.why: Students must "include a brief (2-3 sentence) note explaining how the tool was used, including the prompt or settings", which names prompt and settings details, P25.
units.anchor: include a brief (2–3 sentence) note explaining how the tool was used

units.why: "Undisclosed use of AI tools will be considered a violation of academic integrity", so failure to disclose is itself the violation, P28.
units.anchor: Unauthorized or undisclosed use of AI tools will be considered a violation of academic integrity
units.fit_note: Also treats unauthorized use as a violation and says grade may be affected (not a fixed penalty).

units.why: The text gives the reason for documenting AI use: it "helps you reflect on your learning process and ensures transparency", a rationale for disclosure that no type captures.
units.anchor: helps you reflect on your learning process and ensures transparency in your academic work
units.uncovered_note: Rationale for the disclosure requirement: reflection and transparency.

units.why: Students unsure how to document AI use are told to "reach out or visit the University of Idaho Writing Center", a pointer to human support, P72.
units.anchor: University of Idaho Writing Center

units.why: Option 3 allows AI tools "if that use is properly documented and cited", a permit-with-conditions default, P02.
units.anchor: may be used in this course if that use is properly documented and cited

documents.title: Student Conduct
documents.summary: The Dean of Students conduct page describes the Student Code of Conduct process. AI appears only twice: prohibited AI tools count as academic dishonesty, and students are told to read each syllabus because instructors set different AI limits.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no AI stance of its own; it lists "reliance on prohibited technological assistance/artificial intelligence tools" as dishonesty and says "each instructor may have different limits or expectations of use", so the decision is delegated to instructors.

units.why: The page says "individual instructors may establish additional academic integrity expectations for their courses", leaving AI limits to instructors, P04.
units.anchor: individual instructors may establish additional academic integrity expectations for their courses
units.fit_note: Stated for academic integrity expectations in general; AI is covered by implication and in the later AI line.

units.why: Students are told the instructor guidelines "can vary ... so be sure to review them carefully", a duty to learn each course's rules, P78.
units.anchor: can vary based on subject matter and teaching style
units.fit_note: Applies to academic integrity expectations generally, not AI only.

units.why: Under prohibited behavior in academic dishonesty, the Code lists "reliance on prohibited technological assistance/artificial intelligence tools", classing prohibited AI use as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: reliance on prohibited technological assistance/artificial intelligence tools

units.why: Students are told "each instructor may have different limits or expectations of use. Read your course syllabus carefully!", a duty to find and follow each course's AI rules, P78.
units.anchor: each instructor may have different limits or expectations of use

notes: Coder A rerun, coded from the three included documents only. CETL page is an archived 2025 copy. Skipped as not AI-policy: navigation, news items, the Quick Reads reading list, the alcohol amnesty policy and general conduct-process text on the conduct page, and repeated option text in the syllabus article.
